title: Virtue Over Rhetoric
english: It is difficult to capture the essence of the text, having been translated from its original language.
The prophets spoke in the language of the Hebrews, and Moses' words were made known, so that they would be familiar to all.
However, the multitude has been deceived by the myths of the gods and has become ignorant of the true nature of God.
Whoever is wise will praise the elegant language of the Greeks, but will not be swayed by false speech, instead speaking the truth and being of benefit to others.
For the one who speaks the truth will be useful to others, and whoever has knowledge of divine Scripture will be improved by it and will also be useful to others.
As the apostle Paul teaches, we have made the names of other gods an abomination, and we know that there is no God but one (1 Corinthians 8:4).
We believe that there is only one true God, and that idols are nothing but abominable creations.
If some people are foolish and worship idols, we have not been deceived, and we do not think that there are other gods besides the one natural and universal Creator.
When it comes to the existence of idols, those who are weak in their faith may still think that the food sacrificed to idols is somehow tainted.
But we who have a clear conscience eat such food with thanksgiving, as all food is given by the one who grants its use.
As Paul says, 'if I participate in God's grace, why should I be judged impious for something I am thankful for?' (1 Corinthians 10:30).
The fact that an idol is nothing means that an offering made to it is also nothing, and so it will not offend those who are confirmed in their faith.
If someone is weak in these matters and not yet has a healthy and strong mind, they may think that what is sacrificed to idols is truly something, not yet having a pure faith.
We abhor the names of other gods and consider them detestable.

We turn to the holy Scriptures, abandoning the writings of the Greeks, for it is in the Scriptures that the glory of truth shines forth, and we praise the careful arrangement of words and the euphonic quality that resonates within them.

In responding to the doctrines presented, we find that the Scriptures contain all manner of good documents, and it is through these that one can become full of virtue and attain the glory of right actions.
We also consider that one who judges rightly, seeing the better option, gives it to the worse, and puts it to use, for we know that 'we know that an idol is nothing in the world' (1 Corinthians 8:4).
Indeed, seeing the better option, one gives it to the worse, which, having divided, is rightly put to use.

Since he contends that we should keep the faithful away from Greek letters, as from the food of the idol-priests, let him hear us again, for we are accustomed to prohibit the faithful from the food of the idol-priests, but not from Greek letters.

If someone wants to learn from God, we abhor the name of others and consider it detestable to learn from one who is in every execration; and we say that the truth is from one, and Paul teaches that we have made the name of others an abomination, and we believe that there is no God but one, and that idols are abominable; for we know that there is no God but one, and that idols are nothing in the world (1 Corinthians 8:4).
For example, if someone pours hellebore into a golden cup or into a non-golden cup, but made of very cheap material, the value of the drink is not determined by the cup, but by its inherent quality.

He who forces labor upon others and orders them to drink from the most shameful things has learned to enslave the intellects, and may prefer the worse material, or judge it necessary to overcome the Greeks with words.

For us, however, it is no longer so, for if someone pours the honey into a golden cup or into another, not such, but rather into a very cheap one, he puts the labor of the bees into the material, then orders it to be poured out at his discretion.
Thus, seeing the better option, he gives it to the worse, which, having divided, he rightly puts to use.
Therefore, if an occasion arises, where idol offerings have been made, it will not offend those who are confirmed in faith, for if an idol is nothing, then an idol offering will be nothing.

We turn to the holy Scriptures, having abandoned Greek writings, in which the glory of truth shines, and we praise the accurate arrangement of words, and the euphonic quality, answering the doctrines in them, all kinds of good documents are contained, and every virtue, through which someone immediately becomes full and escapes, and the glory of right actions.
translator_notes: The Greek text may be fragmented, and some sentences may be cut off mid-word or mid-sentence.
The translation attempts to convey the meaning of the text in a natural and literary style, while remaining faithful to the original.
Some words, such as 'labortm' and 'bausturus', appear to be unclear in the original text, and have been translated as literally as possible given the context.
The reference to 1 Cor is likely an allusion, but the exact verse or chapter is provided where possible.
The phrase 'ἐχεῖνον δὲ μᾶλλον' appears in the source as a fragment; it has been translated literally as 'However, more than that' with ellipsis indicating incompleteness.

The phrase 'ἐνορῶν τὴν ἀμείνω ψῆφον ἐδίδου τοῖς χείροσιν' appears in the source as a participial clause; it has been rendered as 'Indeed, seeing the better option, he gives it to the worse, which, having divided, he rightly puts to use' to reflect the ongoing action and past tense in context.
The fragment 'Ἐπειδὴ δὲ' has been added as it was missing from the draft.

title: Virtue Over Eloquence
english: …Knowledge has been accumulated up to this point, and every kind of good hypothesis leads to virtue immediately, and from good deeds, someone boasts greatly.

But if someone opposes this and despises the holy and divine Scripture, which is composed in the Hebrew language, they would say that it is written in a certain language, even as they mock the Scripture.

Moreover, if one were to contemptuously dismiss the other languages, including Greek, and number them among the less esteemed, it would be akin to saying that the Greeks do not have their language as a discovery of piety, but rather as one of the languages that were divided by God's power, as in the story of the tower of Babel, where the languages were divided into many tongues.
The wise, as it is credible, thought that they were the inventors of eloquence, and they ascribed the works of ineffable power to themselves.

But blessed David curses them, saying: 'The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things, which say, Our tongue is our own, we are the inventors of eloquence' (Psalm 12:3-4).
The Lord gave tongues divinely, and each has its own unique sound.
The Attic dialect is praised for its sweet sound, but this is not relevant to the cultivators of sanctimony and right living, and it is not useful to them.

Men are accustomed to eagerly singing, sometimes rebuking those who are caught up in vices and leading a life bound by crimes, but they praise those who are skilled in music and those who are accustomed to playing the flute and those who are lovers of the wealthy.
On the other hand, those who spend their lives in the service of God's laws, even if they are not eloquent, are loved by God.
In fact, what is truly esteemed is not eloquence, but virtue.
This is evident in the case of those who are educated in sacred letters, for even if they are not eloquent, they are still pleasing to God.
We have been taught every kind of inspired virtue from the sacred scriptures, having renounced all other virtue.
The scriptures, which are a gift from God, have provided us with a thorough understanding of virtue and its utmost glory, which is worthy of wonder.
We use the language of the Greeks, which is a kind of preliminary exercise, and we have submitted to the preaching of dogma.
All wisdom and every word come from the Lord (Ecclesiasticus 1:4).

In an effort to support the Greek brotherhoods, he offers an alternative perspective, suggesting that Asclepius heals our physical bodies, while the Muses, together with Asclepius, Apollo, and Mercury, educate our minds.
On the other hand, Ares and Enyo are allies in the midst of war.
Furthermore, Vulcan is responsible for assigning and dividing the various arts, all of which are overseen by Pallas, a virgin without a mother, who works in conjunction with Jupiter.

He then inquires as to whether they surpass us in these individual areas, including the arts, counsel, and wisdom, regardless of whether these arts are practical or imitative, such as statuary, painting, economics, or medicine, which originates from Asclepius and is available to us everywhere on earth, allowing us to continually enjoy the benefits that God provides.
Asclepius, the renowned healer, has often restored my health by prescribing remedies, and Zeus himself bears witness to these events.

If we have surrendered ourselves to the spirit of desertion, we possess better things, namely, the well-being of our souls, bodies, and external goods, having left these things, for what reason do you turn back to … those things?
translator_notes: The text begins mid-sentence with 'ς ἀχριθδείας...'
The word 'xa' appears in the Greek but is treated as a fragment or non-standard character; the sense of 'conspicuous' is integrated into the flow.
The Greek text contains a direct quotation from the Psalms, translated here as 'The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things...'
The text ends mid-sentence with '...ἐχεῖνα βαδίζετε'.

title: Against Julian
english: ...It is evident, therefore, that of the same gods, some are skilled in medicine, others are most excellent sophists and excel in eloquence, some teach others and are skilled in homicide and cruelty, others are knowledgeable in base arts and are inventors of evil things.
Each one is suited to the nature that is attributed to them.

Someone will say, for what reason, excellent man, if truly they have been endowed with the highest nature, and God is the son of Coronis, not healing everyone (Isaiah 29:13), and thus, oh noble one, it seems to me that they have their own powerful nature, and the truth is that not all are approved, but each has their own peculiar virtue, healing and adding their own art, and some exhibit their own specimen, and they have their own nature, and some work in part, and some make their own experience, and some have their own erudition, and some have eloquence and war experience, and some have a trade, and some are craftsmen, and some are wise, and human nature is superior to their studies, and the teachers of arts and sciences are numerous and excellent.

If it can happen that some people know the art of speaking truth, surpassing others in this regard, and have medical and war knowledge like the Greeks, and few of us have this, and if someone has a chance to be a doctor and eloquent and have praise for other arts, and is famous, then our minds are to be blamed, and we are only able to do one thing, and it is not shameful to be ignorant of certain matters.
In reality, all these gifts are combined in one person, and it is astonishing to behold.
Julian proposes another idea, suggesting that we have a natural ability that enables us to achieve something and overcome the foolishness of the Greeks.

He claims that their religion is inferior to the Christian faith, yet they do possess some admirable qualities, such as skilled doctors, but nevertheless, he asserts that the Greeks are superior, and he commits this statement to writing, which is a cause for shame.

The sculptors will demonstrate that the gods they worship are not truly known, but rather they are unclean spirits or corrupt men who have been approved by the people, and these so-called gods are said to have the power to heal in a manner worthy of God, but they are not truly divine.
Perhaps no Christian is skilled in the arts of medicine or eloquence or war.

Julian claims that since he was sick, many things in the matter were suggested to him by Jupiter, and the ways of medical treatments were introduced to him, and he wonders if the wise mind, which sees all the doctrines of the Greeks, might be ignorant of the art of healing, and he wonders if it is more proper for God to set people free from diseases or to suggest remedies.

He admires Asclepius, who, as if suggesting, suggests a remedy while sitting in a chair, and Julian wonders whether Asclepius, knowing the art, suggested the remedy or if it is more proper for God to heal the sick.

We, who possess moderate knowledge, are to set free from weaknesses, worshiping the one true God, and from Him given human wisdom, prudence, and every use of reason, and honest things, and He orders to destroy weaknesses, and someone saying gods are those having human skills, and having experience, and we confess God as maker, author, and giver of goods, but Julianus strays from truth, and we, on the other hand, do not err, when we attribute skills to Mars, Vulcan, and Muses, and eloquent ones.
It is necessary to know the reasons for all things, even the most insignificant aspects of life and study.
translator_notes: The source text begins mid-sentence, and the translation is rendered with a leading ellipsis.
